questions.problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{y}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{y}{x})+1)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{y}{x})+1) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{vx}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{vx}{x})+1) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =v(\operatorname{ln}⁡v+1) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =v\operatorname{ln}⁡v+v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =v\operatorname{ln}⁡v \\ \frac{1}{v\operatorname{ln}⁡v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{v\operatorname{ln}⁡v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{v\operatorname{ln}⁡v}\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

To evaluate the integral on the left-hand side, we use integration by substitution with

$$
u=\operatorname{ln}⁡v,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}=\frac{1}{v}.
$$

We now proceed to solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{v\operatorname{ln}⁡v}\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{u}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}v}\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|u| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡v| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}\,.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡v| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x}| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x}| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{C} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x}| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{C}|x|) \\ |\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x}| & =|x|{e}^{C} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x} & =\pm {e}^{C}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{y}{x} & =Kx \\ \frac{y}{x} & ={e}^{Kx} \\ y & =x{e}^{Kx}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we introduced the new constant of integration:

$$
K=\pm {e}^{C}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{yx}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{yx}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{(vx)x}{(vx)^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{v{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}({v}^{2}+1)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v}{{v}^{2}+1}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v-{v}^{3}-v}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{{v}^{2}+1}{{v}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{v}^{2}+1}{{v}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{{v}^{3}})\,\text{d}v & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|v|-\frac{1}{2{v}^{2}} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡|v|-\frac{1}{{v}^{2}} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2{C}_{1} \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡|v|-\frac{1}{{v}^{2}} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we introduced $C=2{C}_{1}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{y}{x}|-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\frac{y}{x}|+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} & =C \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} & =C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is NOT a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
questions.worked_solution:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is NOT the case is:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{y}^{2}+xy}
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{y}^{2}+xy}.$

We see that the numerator is NOT a homogeneous polynomial. Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is NOT a homogeneous function.

Hence, the original differential equation is  NOT homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{y}^{2}+xy}\,
$$

We can check that this is not homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)\ne f(x,y),$ as follows:

For $x=1$, $y=2$ and $t=3$, for instance, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =f(2\cdot 1,2\cdot 3) \\  & =f(2,6) \\  & =\frac{{2}^{2}+1}{{6}^{2}+2(6)} \\  & =\frac{5}{48}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =f(1,2) \\  & =\frac{{1}^{2}+1}{{2}^{2}+1(2)} \\  & =\frac{2}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, there exists at least one combination of values of $x$, $y$ and $t$ for which the identity $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)$ is not observed.

Hence, the original differential equation is  NOT homogeneous.

questions.knowledge_point: Transforming a Homogeneous Differential Equation into a Separable Equation Using a Substitution
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}-{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+2y{x}^{2}}.
$$

If the transformation $y=v(x)x$ is applied to the differential equation, what is the resulting equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Using the transformation $y=vx$ (where $v=v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given differential equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}-{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+2y{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{3}+x(vx)^{2}-(vx)^{3}}{x(vx)^{2}+2(vx){x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{3}(1+{v}^{2}-{v}^{3})}{{x}^{3}({v}^{2}+2v)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{1+{v}^{2}-{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}+2v} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1+{v}^{2}-{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}+2v}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1+{v}^{2}-{v}^{3}-{v}^{3}-2{v}^{2}}{{v}^{2}+2v} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1-{v}^{2}-2{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}+2v} \\ \frac{{v}^{2}+2v}{1-{v}^{2}-2{v}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{y}{x}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{x}).
$$

If the transformation $y=v(x)x$ is applied to the differential equation, what is the resulting equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Using the transformation $y=vx$ (where $v=v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given differential equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{x}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{vx}{x}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{vx}{x}) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =v-2\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$
